synopsis_paragraphs: Ghost Meets Gal! (Ghost Meets Gal! / ごーすと・みーつ・ぎゃる！) episode 4 sits in the mid-cour inflection, where the premise stops being a pitch. This is not a plot dump. The public catalog pitch is only a floor: a currently airing Japanese television serial with incomplete episode synopses in English catalogs. What the week actually asks is whether AtoriE used that floor as architecture or as wallpaper.

Genres on the tin read Comedy, Fantasy; the useful question is which of those labels got camera time and which were merchandising. Community score currently hovers around an unranked haze, which tells you heat, not craft. We read the episode as a turning-point document: who gained a new obligation, who lost a convenient lie, and whether the cour’s theme got more expensive. Ghost Meets Gal! is being watched as a live product of manga adaptation. Japanese viewers argue about pacing against the source and about whether new episodes add a relationship change or only another demonstration of power. If you only remember a super move, you watched the trailer inside the episode. If you remember a silence, a blocked doorway, or a joke that hurt, you watched the show. Radar note unique to episode 4: this week we grade geography: does episode 4 of Ghost Meets Gal! remember the last location it promised, or did the cour teleport for convenience. Japanese same-night talk usually splits into people who wanted a trailer and people who wanted a scene. We side with the scene. If you are reading this briefing instead of a wiki recap, that is the contract.
sakuga_paragraphs: Seasonal television is a lighting and labor story before it is a lore story. Japanese first-night reactions—quote tweets from sakuga accounts, NicoNico live comments, the slower next-morning recs—usually cluster around three tells: whether action reads, whether faces hold, and whether the episode had a second temperature besides the title card.

Our desk treats those tells as primary sources of reception, not as a substitute for watching. For episode 4 specifically, the desk’s sakuga note is structural: the mid-cour inflection, where the premise stops being a pitch usually exposes whether a studio is spending on the set-piece or on the connective tissue (walks, meals, strategy tables, the extra inhales before violence). Japanese first-night posts still function as a distributed dailies screening. When those posts go quiet, it is not always a pan—sometimes it is a drama week, and drama weeks are graded on faces. When they explode, isolate whether the praise is for a single hero cut or for sequence direction. Only the latter predicts a good cour.
